Diversity-mediated changes in stand structure explain the variability in broadleaf tree species response to drought [SOURCE: Page_132]

Decarsin Renaud^1,2,3,4, Bonal Damien^5, Guillemot Joannès^2,3,6, Rewald Boris^7, Carrière Simon^8, le Maire Guerric^2.3, Loiseau Bertille^8, Simioni Guillaume^1, Veuillen Léa^1, Werner Ramona^7, Martin-StPaul Nicolas^1 [SOURCE: Page_132]

1 INRAE, URFM, Avignon, 84140, France 2 CIRAD, UMR Eco&Sols, Montpellier, 34394, France 3 Eco&Sols, Univ. Montpellier, CIRAD, INRAE, Institut Agro, IRD, Montpellier, 34394, France 4 French Environment and Energy Management Agency, Angers, 49004, France 5 Université de Lorraine, AgroParisTech, INRAE, UMR Silva, Nancy, 54000, France 6 Department of Forest Sciences, ESALQ, University of São Paulo, Piracicaba, 05508- 060, Brazil 7 Institute of Forest Ecology, Department of Forest and Soil Sciences, University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences (BOKU), Gregor-Mendel-Str. 33, 1190 Vienna, Austria 8 UMR METIS, Sorbonne Université, UPMC, CNRS, EPHE, 75005 Paris, France [SOURCE: Page_132]

130 [SOURCE: Page_132]

Abstract Mixing species is increasingly considered as a key management option to adapt forest to climate change. However, we miss a mechanistic understanding of how tree species interactions influence drought response in mixtures. More diverse forest stands are expected to hold a greater diversity of tree forms and generate heterogeneity in tree’s local neighbourhood affecting local growing conditions (e.g temperature, humidity, radiation). This would in turn lead to changes in tree functioning under drought. To test this hypothesis, it appears crucial to monitor multiple physiological indicators of tree response to drought in relation to tree level features (size, forest structure, competition, soil properties). In this study we monitored seasonal water use dynamics (sap flow density), drought stress (water potential, hydraulic safety margins), growth patterns (height and diameter at breast height), and local tree environment (neighbour basal area, size difference to neighbours, competition index, stand LAI and soil conductivity) of seventy-two trees of four different broadleaf species over a gradient of species composition (from monoculture to 4 species mixtures) in a 9 years old plantation during the 2022 summer drought. We show that drought impact on tree physiological functioning was greater in mixtures as compared to pure stands. Convergent patterns of sap flow density response to soil water availability emerged in two-species mixtures, suggesting an indirect effect of the mixture through the structure of the neighbourhood (inherited from the differentiated growth of the species) and the water use strategies of the species. The results of the multivariate analysis indicate that, although the influence of local forest structure on physiological responses was not uniform across species and measured traits, it was a significant factor in determining tree physiological response to drought. This supports the idea that local neighbourhood environment that is inherited from species mixture effects on tree growth at an earlier stage of the plantation partly explains the diversity of individual physiological responses to drought at a given time. [SOURCE: Page_133]

131 [SOURCE: Page_133]

Introduction Anthropogenic global changes have been negatively affecting forest functions and services (Anderegg et al., 2013; Hammond et al., 2022). Mixing tree forest species is increasingly promoted as a nature-based solution to adapt forest to global changes (Messier et al., 2022; Trenberth et al., 2014). Indeed, species diversity is already known to have the potential to improve resilience by promoting stand pest resistance (Jactel et al., 2017), hosting more biodiversity and improving crucial functions such as productivity (Morin et al., 2014) and productivity stability to disturbances (Schnabel et al., 2022). More specifically, functional diversity appears to be the drivers of biodiversity functioning responses (Anderegg et al., 2018; Blondeel et al., 2024; Schnabel et al., 2022). Increasing drought and heat waves appear crucial among threats to forest in the context of global changes (Brodribb et al., 2020; McDowell et al., 2022). Exploring the relationships between trees within the forest and tree species functional diversity on individual drought responses is therefore a very active research field. In fact, it could provide further information on how to support forest restoration and adaptation to climate change. However, the literature is still conflicting on this topic. At global scale, an evaluation of eddy-covariance forest-atmosphere gas exchanges response to drought supported an improved resilience in forests functionally diverse in terms of hydraulic traits (Anderegg et al., 2018). Consistent with this, an analysis based on remotely sensed forest greenness also supported an enhanced drought resistance in more diverse forests (Liu et al., 2022). However local studies have not always confirmed these patterns and the underlying mechanisms remain obscure. Greenhouse experiments on young potted plants have pinpointed that the combination of two species with contrasted level of isohydricity could alleviate drought mortality risk for anisohydric species but with a potential negative impact on the isohydric species (Bello et al., 2019; E. Mas et al., 2024; Moreno et al., 2024). Other controlled experiments emphasized the importance of diversity mediated changes in tree sizes, which could enhance or lower drought stress (Fruleux et al., 2016; Guillemot and Martin-StPaul, 2024; E. Mas et al., 2024). It is expected that an increase in species diversity will enhance stand productivity through an overyielding effect that improves light use efficiency. However, this may also lead to an increase in soil water consumption, potentially causing greater drought stress to the community. Because mixture effect on drought stress can be mediated by changes in local [SOURCE: Page_134]

132 [SOURCE: Page_134]

neighbourhood effects, such as competition and canopy structure (Decarsin et al., 2024; Grossiord, 2020; Martin-Blangy et al., 2023), it also appears crucial to explore how specific combination of species with distinct ecological strategies affect drought stress through changes in local neighbourhood conditions (Mathes et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2022). Yet, field studies that have attempted to evaluate how different levels of mixtures influence drought response at tree to ecosystem scale revealed even much more contrasted patterns (Decarsin et al., 2024; Grossiord, 2020; Haberstroh and Werner, 2022). In a meta-analysis gathering field studies using various indicators of drought responses, Grossiord, 2020 suggested that the magnitude and the direction of the diversity effect is contextual to the specific composition and ultimately depends on each tree local neighbourhood. In another meta-analysis by Haberstroh and Werner, 2022 which focused on ecophysiological indicator of drought stress resistance and resilience (mostly based on sap flow measured at the drought peak or following post-drought re-watering), the authors suggested that drought stress could be alleviated in mixture under mild to severe drought, but that extreme drought could have the opposite effects enhancing drought stress. Conflicting this view, a recent study (Decarsin et al., 2024) -- measuring the hydraulic safety margins during an extreme drought (HSM) on more than 15 species on 5 experimental sites where diversity has been manipulated across Europe-- showed that species diversity and some peculiar compositions can have, both, a very strongly positive or negative effect on drought stress and drought mortality risk. These results are potentially explained by composition mediated canopy structure and microclimate buffering. Indeed, in a forest ecosystem, the occurrence of tree species with different drought resistance traits, water use strategies, growth rates and root or canopy anatomy is expected to modify local microclimate conditions (Zhang et al., 2022), thus affecting individual tree sap flow density, drought stress and growth either in well-watered or drought conditions (Grossiord et al., 2014, 2013; Kunert et al., 2011; Lübbe et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2024). Altogether these studies call for a better mechanistic understanding of how some specific assemblage of species with different strategies and traits can lead to differences in drought stress patterns. Furthermore, gaining a better understanding of the mechanisms driving individual functioning under drought in mixed stands remains a major challenge and this knowledge could not only improve how dynamic vegetation models simulate these interactions, but also guide the design of resilient plantations and forest restoration programs. The divergence in the results reported in different 133 [SOURCE: Page_135]

meta-analyses indicate a need for an evaluation of the mixture effect on drought stress based on multiple drought stress metrics. Approaches to better understanding how the actual tree-to-tree interactions alter drought stress rely on direct measures of tree water status. Sap flow sensor is a well-documented method to monitor tree sap flow density at a high temporal resolution. The analysis of both ecophysiological indicators, whether measured at a single point in time (i.e., water potential) or over a period of time (sap flow density), is crucial for understanding the processes involved in drought stress resilience. In this present study we aimed at evaluating how mixing tree species with different ecological strategies influence drought stress and how this can be mediated by changes in local neighbourhood conditions (tree size, competition, canopy structure, soil heterogeneity). Drought responses were assessed both dynamically through continuous measurements of sap flow density and at the drought peak using water potential and hydraulic safety margins. The study was conducted in an experimental forest plantation established in 2013, including four tree species (Norway maple, Acer platanoides; the small-leaved lime, Tilia cordata; common hornbeam, Carpinus betulus, Pedunculate oak, Quercus robur) (Werner et al 2024). The experimental site includes monocultures, two types of two-species mixtures and a four species mixture. We first tested the species richness effect on (1) trees and neighbouring structural responses over growth (i.e, diameter, height, neighbour basal area, competition indices, size heterogeneity) and (2) physiological responses (WET, DRY and ReWET sap flow density, resistance, recovery and predawn and midday water potentials) before, during and after an extreme drought event. [SOURCE: Page_136]

134 [SOURCE: Page_136]

Material & Methods [SOURCE: Page_137]

Site description, climate conditions and studied species [SOURCE: Page_137]

The study was conducted during the vegetation period of the year 2022 (from 22/03/2022 to 13/11/2022) at the B-Tree experimental forest plantation site (BOKU University, Austria) which is part of the Tree Diversity Network (TreeDivNet). The BTree experiment is situated in Tulln, which is in the alluvial basin of the Danube River in the North East of Austria (48°19'3.625"N, 16°4'0.815"E). It was planted in 2013 in a hexagonal design with one-meter distance between each tree. This experimental tree biodiversity plantation consists of monocultures and mixtures of four species, Quercus robur (Qr), Carpinus betulus (Cb), Acer platanoides (Ap) and Tilia cordata (Tc), which are all typical of the warm lowland forests of Austria. These species differ in terms of resource use, with Acer and Carpinus being the most acquisitive and Tilia and Quercus the most conservatives, as indicated by previous studies (Werner et al., 2024) and ecological traits collected from the literature (Serrano-León et al., 2024; Table S$_2$). The design was made to test the effect of tree diversity on growth, water relations, rhizosphere diversity and carbon sequestration. The plantation is composed of three diversity levels in seven plot types (4 monocultures, 2 mixtures with two species, and 1 mixture with four species) which are replicated twice (Figure 1a). The two species- mixtures involve only two combinations of species, either Ap-Tc or Qr-Cb, as the initial design of the plantation was to test the interactions between species with contrasted behaviours (acquisitive vs. conservative). The soil type is moist Chernozem; the soil is hydromorphic, humus-rich and contains free calcium carbonate, originating from Danube sediments. The soil has a pH of 8.28 ± 0.01, and a C to nitrogen ratio of 19.7 ± 0.7 in the topsoil (0–20 cm). A thin (<1–2 mm) layer of organic material (Litter and Fermentation Horizon) developed on top of the mineral soil during the experiment. For more details on soil properties, see (Werner et al., 2024). [SOURCE: Page_137]

Tree sampling and drought stress metrics [SOURCE: Page_138]

Sap flow density measurements We used sap flow density measurement during the 2022 vegetative season to study species richness effect on the two components of tree drought resilience (i.e, resistance and recovery, sensu Haberstroh and Werner, 2022). This vegetation season included a well-watered period followed by a severe drought, then a recovery dynamic period, and finally a well-watered, post-recovery period. During the last week of May 2022, we equipped seventy-two trees from the four different species and four different treatments with sap flow sensors. We used the so-called Granier type heat dissipation probes (Granier, 1985) that were either home-made or bought at UP- System GmBH (Ibbenbüren, Germany) to assess sap flow density (SFD, L.dm-2.h-1). [SOURCE: Page_138]

136 [SOURCE: Page_138]

Each sensor was inserted in the trunk at about 1-m height. We used six replicates per species and treatment, making a total of twenty-four individuals in each treatment (monocultures, two species mixtures, and four species mixture). Trees were selected based on the following size and ecological criteria: (1) trees with a diameter at 1-m high over 4 cm to allow sensor installation, (2) trees with good sanitary state to limit that sensor installation would harm tree functioning, (3) trees needed to be dominant or codominant for each species in each plot to maximise tree interactions, (4) first crown neighbourhood species composition had to be as close as the theoretical plot species composition ratio and a measured tree couldn’t be in the first crown neighbourhood to limit artefactual covariations over trees. All sensors were north exposed and covered with a thermic and rain isolation cover to avoid thermal gradient (through direct sun, ambient heat or water flow on the bark) that would alter measurements. Data were recorded every ten seconds with CR1000 or CR800 data logger (Campbell Scientific Inc, Loughborough, Leicestershire, UK) and thirty-minute averages were computed. Individual daily sums of sap flow density (L.dm-2.d-1) were calculated and used in the analyses. Because of sensor failure, one Acer tree had to be removed from the analyses. The first week of measurements was not considered in order to ensure a full stabilisation of the signal. Four days (from day 231 to 234) had also been removed from the analysis because of important rain events, altering the temperature signal. We used individual time series of daily sums of sap flow density to compute different indicators of tree functioning under well-watered, dry, recovery and post recovery well-watered conditions. Sap flow density variation was characterised as follows. We summarised individual sap flow density of the well- watered period (WET), the DRY period and the ReWET period. These periods were defined by species with the first and the last day of the period being the days showing the maximum and minimum SFD among individuals of the considered species. Then we calculated SFD_WET, SFD_DRY and SFD_ReWET as the individual mean on every period. The resistance and recovery terms were individually calculated as the linear slope response to relative extractable water (REW), modelled with the tree hydraulic model Sureau, from the day of maximum SFD during the WET period to the day of minimum SFD during the DRY period and from the day of maximum SFD during the DRY period to the day of maximum SFD during the ReWET period. These two individual flow density responses to REW addresses how trees respond to water [SOURCE: Page_139]

137 [SOURCE: Page_139]

availability change over a drying event and a rewetting event. The higher this term is, the higher the response to available water in fast. Water potential and hydraulic safety margins We measured water stress three times across the monitored period. We measured predawn and midday water potentials of the 72 monitored trees on days 187, 205 and 244 (6th of July, 24th of July and 1st of September). Sunlit leaves or shoots were sampled using pole pruners. WPpd was measured in a two hours slot before sunrise and WPmd was measured in a two hours slot around solar midday on the same trees. Samples collected were south-oriented. Samples were immediately sealed in plastic Ziplock bags after blowing in it to saturate it with humidity. The samples were then placed in a portable cooler (avoiding contact with ice) in the dark before being measured with the Scholander pressure bomb directly in the field (i.e., less than half an hour after sampling, Rodriguez-Dominguez et al., 2022). [SOURCE: Page_140]

Ancillary data to explore drought and local neighbourhood conditions [SOURCE: Page_140]

In order to understand how drought stress effect on species diversity can be influenced by local conditions and drought dynamics, we relied on various data measured and modelled. [SOURCE: Page_140]

Tree size, canopy structure and competition indices In order to explore the role of individual tree properties and neighbourhood relationship on tree physiological functioning in mixture and monoculture, we used forest inventory data to characterise individual trees morphology and potential neighbourhood interactions. We used the systematic inventory realised during the winter of years 2021-2022, when tree diameter at breast height (dbh) and tree height were measured. In addition to height and dbh, different indicators of competition, and neighbourhood interaction were computed. 𝐵𝐴B , where BA is the basal area, k is one neighbouring tree and n is the total number of immediate neighbouring trees. [SOURCE: Page_141]

Spatio-temporal variations of soil properties [SOURCE: Page_141]

To characterize spatio-temporal variations in soil properties, we combined geophysical approaches, conventional moisture probe monitoring, and ecophysiological modelling. Geophysical approaches are ideal for characterizing the spatial variability of soil properties at plot scale (Carrière et al., 2020; Loiseau et al., 2023). Electromagnetic induction (EMI) was performed with a CMD-mini-explorer device, which provides an integrated signal over the 0-1.8 m depth range. This technique was used to obtain a map describing the spatial heterogeneity of soil, such as moisture content, rock fraction or depth of the gravel layer (Carrière et al., 2020). In this study, EMI mapping was measured once during wet conditions and before the vegetation period (20/03/2022) to limit spatial variability related to soil water consumption by trees. In this context soil conductivity assessed through EMI could mimic soil thickness. Electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) was carried out using an ABEM Terrameter with 64 electrodes spaced 0.75 m apart. This technique enabled a more detailed description of vertical variability with vertical 2D geoelectric cross-sections (Loiseau et al 2020). We then installed four 48 m transects crossing the different experimental plots with attention to minimise the distance to each monitored tree. We used the differential in ERT in monocultures between the wettest and the driest measured date as a proxy of the depth of the rooting system of the different species (REF). Temporal variations in resistivity were used to describe differences in water dynamics along the profile. However, the limited number of repetitions did not allow us to convert the ERT [SOURCE: Page_141]

139 [SOURCE: Page_141]

signal into water content (Loiseau et al. submitted). However, we were able to characterize the consistency of resistivity trends with the dynamics monitored locally by the moisture probes (data not shown). The B-Tree site was also equipped with time domain reflectometry (TDR) sensors positioned on a regular grid (every 6 metres) allowing it to monitor moisture content over 0-60 cm depth through manual measurements (Trase System 1; SoilMoisture, CA, USA). During the study period TDR measurements were done six times across the vegetation period (DOY X, Z, Z). We extracted the moisture content data from the closest TDR probe to each tree equipped with sap flow sensors. These data were used to compute individual tree metrics of moisture content. Some correlations between moisture content variability from TDR and soil conductivity from EMI indicated that EMI can partly assess soil moisture variability (Figure S$_2$). To explore potential differences among species in the patterns of soil water withdrawals from the ground, we equipped the site with an electrical resistivity transect (ERT) of 48-meter-long crossing all monocultures located at the Northern part of the Site (Figure 1). ERT is a classical geophysical method that can be used to monitor soil water dynamics (Loiseau et al 2024, under review) at different depths. ERT electrodes were positioned every 0.75m allowing to explore soil conductivity down to 10m. ERT was monitored at 5 dates during the 2022 vegetation season including one date during the well-watered period and one date during the dry period. In this study we used the relative variation in ERT between the wet and the dry period to explore the root exploration depth of each species in monoculture (see figure S$_3$). Finally, to obtain a time series of relative soil moisture content that we can use to analyse the sap flow response to drought, we used the relative extractable water (REW) computed with the SurEau model (Ruffault et al., 2022) over the timespan of the experiment as in (Decarsin et al., 2024). [SOURCE: Page_142]

Statistical analysis [SOURCE: Page_142]

We explored how species diversity affected tree growth properties, competition, tree drought stress (HSM, SFD_Dry) and tree sap flow density response to drought. First, for each species, we tested how different species richness changed canopy structure, growth and drought response indicators compared to monoculture using one-way ANOVA on variables computed at the individual level. A significant P-value threshold was set at 0.05. Second, we evaluated how sap flow density response to soil moisture (REW from SurEau model) was influenced by the different composition using mixed [SOURCE: Page_142]

140 [SOURCE: Page_142]

models. We evaluated sap flow density variations for the drying and rewetting phase separately. Indeed, as observed on Figure 1, a first drying phase (early to late summer) shows a monotonic decrease in sap flow density and a distinct rewetting phase (late summer to autumn) showed an increase in SFD with REW increase (Figure 1). We thus separated the dataset in two parts, one corresponding to the drying phase from day to day and one corresponding to a “recovery” phase from day to day. Then for these two periods and for each species, we explore separately the effect of two species mixtures and four species mixtures compared to monoculture. We built linear mixed models using the package lme^4 (lmer function) to evaluate the differences of predicted linear response of sap flow density to REW in the different species richness treatments and for the drying and rewetting phase, as follows: 𝑙𝑚𝑒𝑟(𝑆𝐹𝐷~ 𝑆𝑝𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑒𝑠 𝑟𝑖𝑐ℎ𝑛𝑒𝑠𝑠 ∗ 𝑅𝐸𝑊 + (1|𝑡𝑟𝑒𝑒;: )) where 𝑡𝑟𝑒𝑒;: is the tree unique identity set as a random effect to account for individual repeated daily SFD. Finally we used a principal component analysis (PCA) to explore the coordination of the effects of species richness on trees physiology (SFD and water potential), trees morphology (height and diameter) and neighbourhood structure (i.e, soil conductivity, competition indices, NBA and shading indices). All analysis and figures were produced using the R software ( v. 4.3.1, R core team 2021). [SOURCE: Page_143]

Results [SOURCE: Page_143]

Mixture effects on tree level structural features: size, growth, neighbourhood structure and local soil conditions [SOURCE: Page_143]

For each study species, we explored how mixture treatments affected tree size, growth, neighbourhood conditions (competition, shading) and soil conditions (Figure 2). Overall, we found relatively few significant effects of mixture on tree level properties and relatively large interindividual variability in many tree level features in particular neighbourhood conditions (NBA, Comp^2, Shading crown position, see figure 2). However, a few patterns can be detected. For instance, Tilia cordata (Tc) trees were higher (although but not significantly larger) in mixture with Acer platanoides (Ap) and in the four-species-mixture, than in the monoculture. Ap were larger in mixture with Tc and smaller in the four-species-mixture than in monoculture. Tc neighbourhood was characterised by a slightly higher tree basal area in the two-species-mixture but more [SOURCE: Page_143]

141 [SOURCE: Page_143]

importantly Tc was systematically height dominated in mixture. Quercus robur (Qr) presented some similar trends as Tc in mixtures, as Qr trees were larger in the two species mixture and tended to be higher in mixture than in the monoculture. Similarly, there was a trend for Qr trees to be more height dominated in the four species mixture compared to monoculture. Carpinus betulus (Cb) did not show much trends in response to mixture in terms of growth and size. However, for Cb, mixtures tended to lower the basal area of the neighbours and the competition index compared to monoculture. The soil properties (assessed through soil conductivity) did not change much between mixture treatments, except for Tc where we found a gradually lower conductivity in two and four species mixtures compared to monoculture. Qr presented a slightly higher conductivity in two-species-mixture compared to the monoculture. [SOURCE: Page_144]

Figure 2: Effect of mixture on tree level structural features (size, growth, neighbourhood and soil properties) for the different species as compared to the monoculture. Significance level of mixture treatment compared to the monoculture are indicated upon or below the bars (. <0.1, *<0.05, **< 0.005, *** <0.0005) [SOURCE: Page_144]

Mixture effects on static physiological indicators of drought responses [SOURCE: Page_144]

We defined different static physiological indicators of tree drought responses from sap flux density and water potential measurements which are presented on Figure 3. Species richness treatments trigger a few effects on tree physiological responses [SOURCE: Page_144]

142 [SOURCE: Page_144]

assessed through sap flux density (SFD) or to water potential that differed between species and mixtures (Figure 3). Tc is the species which responded the most significantly to species richness treatments. In the mixture with Ap and in the four species-mixture SFD tended to be lower both during the well-watered conditions (SFD_wet) and the driest conditions (SFD_dry) compared to monoculture. However, no trend was found on SFD measured after the drought release (SFD_rewet) for this species. Consistently, Tc water potential (at predawn and midday) was significantly higher in mixtures (with Ap and in the four-species mixtures). Regarding SFD indicators, Ap tended to show an opposite trend to Tc, with greater values in mixture with Tc, but no trend was found in four species mixtures. Contrary to SFD, water potential data indicated a trend toward greater stress in mixture with Tc and in the four species-mixture. The water stress of Qr did not change significantly across species richness treatments. However, we observed a lower sap flow density in the four species-mixture at the dryer phase. Finally, Cb was more stressed in the two species- mixture as shown by higher (absolute values) midday water potential. Resistance and recovery did not significantly respond to species richness. Nonetheless we observed some trends for these traits (p-value threshold 0.1) indicating that Ap and Qr have higher resistance values in the two species-mixtures in contrast with Tc and Cb which have lower resistance values in two species-mixtures. [SOURCE: Page_145]

Mixture effects on the dynamic response of sap flux density drought installation and drought release [SOURCE: Page_146]

For each species we analysed the SFD response to soil drought (taken as soil relative extractable water, REW) in interaction with the diversity treatment. Each diversity treatment was compared to monoculture separately using a mixed model. Only results using REW computed with the SurEau model are reported here. The analysis was performed both during the establishment of drought and during drought release. Results are reported in Figure 4 and Figure 5 respectively. In the models, the effect of REW was significant in 14 out of 16 comparisons, indicating a clear soil drought effect on SFD both during the drought establishment and recovery period (figure 4 and 5). The mixture treatment was barely significant alone (4 out of 16 comparisons, see figure 4 and 5), however an effect of the interaction diversity treatment and REW was significant for some species in some treatments (11 out of 16 comparisons, see Fig. 4 144 [SOURCE: Page_146]

and 5). We found a significant effect of the interaction in the comparison of monoculture to two species-mixtures for three of the studied species (Ap, Tc and Cb). On the one hand, both Ap and Qr showed a significant increase of the slope of response to soil drought in mixture (p=0.038 and p=0.051), indicating an increased sensitivity to drought, in the two species-mixture. On the other hand, both Tc and Cb showed a significant decrease in the slope of response to drought (p <0.05), indicating a reduced sensitivity to drought, in the two species-mixture (figure 4, first line). Compared to monoculture, treatment effects were generally less pronounced in the four species-mixture treatment than in the two-species treatment, as neither Ap, Tc or Cb showed any change in sap flow density sensitivity to drought. Only Qr showed a significant effect of the four species richness on drought sensitivity. Furthermore, the slope was reduced compared to monoculture, indicating a reduced sensitivity to drought. Neither Ap and Cb showed a species richness effect on sap flux density. Qr and Tc species showed a reduction of sap flow density in the four species-mixture (p = 0.03 and p=0.03). [SOURCE: Page_147]

Figure 4: Predicted sap flow density (obtained (from mixed linear models) response to REW and species richness treatment, for every species during the recovery (i.e., ReWET) phase of the dynamic. The responses were obtained from mixed linear models. During the post drought recovery phase, soil drought and treatment effects did not fully match the patterns found during the drought establishment phase. Tilia cordata (Tc) showed the least response to REW during the recovery phase, in particular in monoculture. Recovery was however significantly more pronounced in two and four species mixtures for this species. Ap and Qr seemed to also recover better in the two [SOURCE: Page_147]

145 [SOURCE: Page_147]

species-mixture. In contrast Qr recovered less in four species, leading to a lower sap flow density for higher values of REW (see figure 3). Ap in the four species-mixture behaves similarly to monoculture. When Cb behaved the same in the two species- mixture compared to the monoculture it recovered less in the four species-mixture tending to a lower sap flow density for higher values of REW. [SOURCE: Page_148]

Figure 5: Predicted sap flow density response to REW and species richness treatment, for every species during the recovery (i.e., ReWET) phase of the dynamic. The responses were obtained from mixed linear models. [SOURCE: Page_148]

Mixture effects on the coordination between tree level environmental conditions and ecophysiological drought responses [SOURCE: Page_148]

A principal component analysis (PCA, figure 6) was made for each species separately, in order to represent the coordination between both tree level structural features (i.e. size, competition, soil) and the physiological drought responses indicators (water potential, SFD, and SFD response to drought) and their structuration across diversity treatments. The two first dimensions of the PCA explained 56.9, 57.1, 56.3 and 51% of the total variance of Acer platanoides(Ap), Tilia cordata (Tc), Quercus robur (Qr) and Carpinus betulus (Cb), respectively. For Acer platanoides (Ap), species richness ellipsoids were overlapping, suggesting similar behaviour among treatments. In contrast, for the other species, ellipsoids were mostly separated indicating a structuration of species richness other the two axes of the PCA. Globally, drought stress metrics were structured over different axes but systematically suggested dominant trees, both in height and diameter, were overstressed. In fact, sap flow [SOURCE: Page_148]

146 [SOURCE: Page_148]

density data were mainly aligned with height related variables (height, shading, crown position). In contrast hydraulic stress (HSMmin and WPpd) were essentially structured with DBH, NBA, comp^2 and soil conductivity. For Tilia cordata (Tc), drought stress metrics (HSM, WPpd and SFD_DRY) were mainly structured along with soil conductivity, canopy structure (shading and crown position), competition (NBA) and DBH on the first axis (36.3% of variance). In addition, we noted that individuals from monocultures tend to differentiate from mixtures on this first axis suggesting complex intra- and inter-specific interactions both due to canopy structure as well as individual tree morphology. Sap flow density during a well-watered period (SFD_WET and SFD_ReWET) were essentially associated with individual tree height. For Quercus robur (Qr), drought stress (HSM, PSi) and sap flow-based drought responses metrics (SFD_dry etc..), were mainly structured on the first axis (32.3% of the variation) along with soil conductivity and canopy structure (shading and crown position). By contrast, competition (comp^2, NBA) and size (DBH and height) metrics were more aligned with the second axis, which encompass 25% of the variance. Furthermore, we noted that individuals from monocultures tended to differentiate from mixture on this competition and size based second axis, thus without much impact on physiological responses. For Carpinus betulus (Cb), drought stress (HSMmin, WPpd) and drought response metrics (recovery and resistance) were mainly structured along with soil conductivity and height related metrics (respectively height and shading) as well as SFD in well- watered conditions. By contrast SFD_DRY was aligned with competition metrics (comp^2 and NBA) and DBH. [SOURCE: Page_149]

147 [SOURCE: Page_149]

Figure 6: PCA results for the different species studied. Only the first two dimensions are shown as they encompass most of the variation (third axe never explained more than 15%). Coloured ellipses help visualise the variability and clustering of individuals around the group centre of a species richness, points and ellipse in red correspond to individuals in monoculture, green correspond to trees in two species richness and blue correspond to trees in four species mixture. Each individual is projected onto the two-dimensional map, and the shape of the dots represents species richness. See figure S$_4$ for pairwise corrplot including all variables for every species. [SOURCE: Page_150]

148 [SOURCE: Page_150]

Discussion [SOURCE: Page_151]

Exploring mixture effect on drought responses [SOURCE: Page_151]

Moderate mixture effects on physiological drought response can be explained by large interindividual variability in tree conditions triggered by mixture In this study we explored the effect of mixing tree species with contrasted ecological strategies on tree physiological functioning during a summer drought. The growth performance of the different species, along with their functional traits (Table S$_1$), indicated that the four species can be positioned along an acquisitive-fast growing vs conservative-slow growing axis. On the one hand of this axis, Acer platanoides (Ap) and Quercus robur (Qr) were the fastest growing and the most acquisitives, and on the other hand, Carpinus betelus (Cb) and Tilia cordata (Tc) were the most conservatives and slow growing species relative to the two species mixture compositions (Ap-Tc and Qr-Cb). We explored how combining these species by pairs of fast growing and slow-growing (Ap-Tc, Qr-Cb), or altogether in a four species mixture (Ap-Tc-Qr-Cb) impacted drought responses, using different physiological indicators of drought responses computed from sap flow density (SFD) time series and tree level features (including tree size, neighbourhood conditions and soil properties). Overall, by using static physiological drought indicators extracted from SFD measured at tree level (SFD_dry, SFD_wet, SFD_rewet), we found relatively modest effects of mixture on drought responses. This is consistent with the large interindividual variability in tree conditions that we reported, and more generally this converges with numerous studies indicating modest and divergent mixture effects on drought responses (Decarsin et al., 2024; Grossiord, 2020; Haberstroh and Werner, 2022). It is likely that the increased heterogeneity in environmental conditions triggered by mixture under field conditions is responsible for large variability in drought responses making it difficult to detect significant signals with the relatively low sample size affordable in ecophysiological studies. [SOURCE: Page_151]

149 [SOURCE: Page_151]

Mixing two species with contrasted resource use strategies led to convergent SFD drought responses compared to monoculture and implications for species performance in mixture Our data revealed consistent patterns in SFD response to mixture, in particular when confronting monocultures and two-species mixtures. In the two-species-mixture, the combination of fast growing (acquisitive) and slow growing (conservative) species led to convergent drought responses when comparing with monocultures. For instance, the slow growing Tilia cordata (Tc) exhibited lower SFD during drought in mixtures than in monoculture, and this trend was particularly pronounced in two-species- mixture with the fast-growing and acquisitive Acer platanoides (Ap).          Ap, on the contrary, exhibited greater SFD than in monoculture when mixed with Tc. Although the statistical tests were not systematically significant, results show a similar pattern when considering the slow growing Carpinus betulus (Cb) which tended to show lower SFD when in mixture with relatively more acquisitive Quercus robur (Qr). Such physiological drought responses to mixtures appeared even stronger when exploring the dynamic responses of SFD to soil drought during drought establishment (Figure 4). When a slow-growing species (Tc, Cb) was grown in mixture with a species growing faster (Ap, Qr), the slow growing species tended to exhibit lower SFD and/or lower responses to soil water deficit compared to monoculture. On the contrary the relatively faster growing and more acquisitive species (Ap, Qr) tended to exhibit higher SFD and steeper slope of response to available soil water when grown along with more conservative’s species (Tilia and Quercus). Assuming that sap flow density is a good proxy for instantaneous productivity, these results indicate that in a mixture of acquisitive and conservative species, faster growing-acquisitive species benefit from being mixed under well-watered conditions, but in turn are penalized during drought, as they experience higher flux decline with soil drought. On the contrary, for slow growing-conservative species, mixtures result in a reduced sap flow density during well-watered conditions, but slow down the pace of response to soil drought, therefore maintaining high productivity for longer periods under harsher conditions. Such a pattern of drought responses which is predictable from the growth strategies selected for the mixture is consistent with forest dynamics expectations (Volaire, 2018). In the following we discuss the probable ecological mechanisms driving these changes. [SOURCE: Page_152]

150 [SOURCE: Page_152]

Differences in tree status and size, inherited from past growth and/or soil properties, can explain SFD drought responses in two species mixtures. For Ap and Tc, SFD differed between species richness all along the gradient of soil water depletion, including during well-watered conditions, which indicates that changes in canopy exposure to ambient conditions (light and VPD) from monoculture to mixture could be a trigger for such differential physiological functioning. In other word, those species which were dominated in mixtures – like Tc which was more shaded in both the two and the four species mixtures – likely have a fewer proportion of sun-exposed leaves, leading to lower transpiration rates and therefore a lower SFD response to soil water depletion during drought establishment. The opposite would occur for acquisitive Ap trees in two species mixtures, where bigger and over-crop Tc trees. This would have led to more leaves and more sun-exposed leaves in two species mixture and thus greater initial SFD and faster soil depletion. This is consistent with the different strategies and traits of the two species (Table 1), as well as with the differential growth and shading status that we measured (Figure 2), and overall indicates that differential size tree status and canopy position, inherited from growth differences at younger stages of the plantation, can be responsible for changes in SFD drought response in mixture compared to monoculture. Nevertheless, we must acknowledge that part of the differential drought responses between treatment could also be related to variability in the local soil conditions at this site. This might particularly be the case for Tc, which is the species most affected by mixture: we indeed observed a significant decrease in soil conductivity from monoculture to the 2 and 4 species mixtures, which might have influenced the growth and the drought responses of this species. This finding highlights the need to progress on the characterisation of the variability in soil conditions to better understand drought stress as recently highlighted (Loiseau et al., 2023). For Quercus robur (Qr) and Carpinus betulus (Cb), we observed more nuanced changes in SFD responses when comparing two-species mixtures with monocultures, which were similarly reflected in tree-level characteristics such as growth, competition, and neighbourhood structure. This can be explained by the similar drought response strategy and size of these two species at the time of this study, as compared to the Ap-Tc couple. Yet, we noticed that Cb experienced significantly reduced competition when mixed with Qr than in monoculture, which might have let them have greater water resources and thus would [SOURCE: Page_153]

151 [SOURCE: Page_153]

have triggered higher water consumption (i.e. higher SFD WET) and thus greater SFD decline during drought. For Qr, the greater SFD drought-induced decline in two- species-mixture was not clearly associated with differential canopy position, shading conditions, crown position or the competition index (Figure 2). However, it must be noticed that Qr trees sampled in the two species mixture grew on more conductive soils and were larger (i.e. bigger DBH) than in monocultures. Changes in tree growth or allometry, maybe related to more fertile soil conditions, may have triggered the observed changes in SFD and the drought responses of Qr in the two species- mixtures. This result thus deserves further evaluation and highlights again the need to explore the spatial heterogeneity in soil conditions. [SOURCE: Page_154]

Species drought responses in four species mixtures were much subtle than in two species mixtures [SOURCE: Page_154]

Species drought responses differed less in the highest level of diversity than in the two species mixture compared to monoculture. There are two possible explanations for this result. On the one hand, the greater overlap in the growth and resource use strategies among species would tend to dampen the strength of the interactions among them, as compared to those in the two-species mixtures. Yet, on the other hand, the higher heterogeneity in tree structure triggered by more numerous strategies could also trigger a greater variability in tree drought responses. In our case the similar variances in tree level structural features found between treatments support the first hypothesis. This is also consistent with the fact that the two species mixture were designed to include the most distinct ecological strategies and thus emphasized species interactions effects. Nonetheless, some changes merit close attention. For instance, the slowest-growing and more conservative species (Tc) was dominated by the three other species in the four species mixture, as in the two species mixtures, and presented a very similar response than in the two species mixture. In contrast, the responses of Qr and Cb in the four species mixtures were slightly modified as compared to those in the two species mixtures, probably because they were partly dominated by Ap in the four species mixture. In line with the results found in two species mixtures, our data support that mixing species with distinct growth strategies triggers changes in morphology and local neighbourhood conditions which in turn impact the physiological functioning of these trees. Interestingly, and in addition to what has been observed in recent drought experiments on young plants (eg. Moreno [SOURCE: Page_154]

152 [SOURCE: Page_154]

et al. 2024; Mas et al. 2023) where hydraulic traits were found mainly responsible for predictable patterns, we found that it is the differences in resource use strategy and growth that led to differences in local structure and morphology between the mixtures, that are responsible for the patterns observed. This is in line with the conclusions of several other studies (Guillemot and Martin-StPaul, 2024; Eugénie Mas et al., 2024) which suggested that growth dynamics were fundamental for predicting water stress dynamics. However, we must acknowledge that when we aimed at understanding the patterns of response in the four-species composition, the trends were less clear; this clearly calls for additional studies and data (e.g. structure and phenology) to correctly understand these patterns. [SOURCE: Page_155]

Exploring mixture effects on drought recovery [SOURCE: Page_155]

The ability of trees to recover after a drought is a key aspect of resilience that can be explored using continuous sap flow data, but is still poorly studied (Haberstroh and Werner, 2022). The few examples in the literature which explored post-drought recovery were based on sap flow at a single post-drought period (Haberstroh et al., 2021; Magh et al., 2020). These studies suggest a delayed or a decreased recovery in mixtures as compared to monocultures. Here, we found lower slopes of SFD post drought recovery compared to monoculture only for Qr and Cb in the four species mixtures (Figure 5). Decrease in SFD recovery can be explained by two main interacting processes. First, greater water stress at the peak of drought could alter hydraulic conductance thereby altering the capacity of SFD to recover after drought. Second, leaf senescence triggered by the decrease of photoperiod in interaction with drought stress (Delpierre et al., 2016) could also reduce the ability of SFD to recover. Since we did not measure leaf phenology or post-drought water potential, we were not able to separate the potential role of these two mechanisms. Nonetheless, we also found faster recovery for some species in the two species mixtures (Ap, Tc, Qr) and in the four species mixture (Tc), as compared to monocultures (Figure 5). In particular, the recovery of Tc in the mixture was particularly faster, albeit the fact they experienced greater drought stress (as measured by both HSM and SFD_dry). One explanation is that trees in monocultures experienced earlier leaf fall than in mixtures and were thus unable to recover. Alternatively, it is possible that Tc trees in mixtures beneficiated additional direct sunlight during late summer fall compared to monoculture – due for instance to phenological shift between species – which would [SOURCE: Page_155]

153 [SOURCE: Page_155]

be consistent with the greater recovery experienced by this species in four species mixture compared to the two species mixture. [SOURCE: Page_156]

Considering various drought stress metrics [SOURCE: Page_156]

In a recent meta-analysis, Haberstroh and Werner, 2022 concluded a generally negative effect of species mixture during severe to extreme drought (SPEI <-1.5) by using sap flow density (SFD) measured at the peak of the drought as a drought stress metric. Interestingly, sap flow density data recorded here do not fully confirm such a pattern (Figure 3). The reason for this could be a lower drought severity at our site. Indeed SPEI$_3$ was ca. -1.2 during the study period which correspond to a moderate drought in 2022 compared to cases considered in Haberstroh and Werner, 2022 review (Table^2 from Haberstroh and Werner, 2022 : Drought classification after McKee et al., 1993 using the Standardised Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010)). However, by using Hydraulic Safety Margins (HSM) measured at the drought peak, we found an increase of drought stress in mixtures consistent with their conclusion (Haberstroh & Werner 2022) in extreme drought. One of the reasons why HSM differed more between treatment than SFD_dry can be that HSM is based on water potential which is a direct indicator of tree water status. In line with this idea, SFD encompasses more information than only drought stress (stomatal and hydraulic conductance to light, VPD and temperature), which could blur its ability to reliably indicate the water status of trees in various drought conditions. This is consistent with the relatively poor correlation between SFD_Dry and HSM that we observed here (Figure S$_2$). In addition, as discussed earlier, we noticed that some significant differences in SFD_DRY (e.g. Ap and Tc) between compositions were already present during the well-watered period (i.e. on SFD_WET). Such observations suggest that using SFD_dry as a single drought stress metric could easily lead to misinterpreting the observed differences when not considering tree functioning before the onset of drought. Actually, using the full sequence of SFD variations along drought could be more appropriate to dynamically examine how water use is regulated throughout drought establishment and later, during drought release (see next section) for the different species in different compositions. However, these two different indices (SFD, HSM) provide a complementary view of the mechanisms of drought stress as supported by our multivariate analysis which explores the coordination between diverse drought response indices and structural indicators at the individual scale [SOURCE: Page_156]

154 [SOURCE: Page_156]

(Figure 6). On the one hand, we observed a general trend for size and/or canopy position indices to influence water use related drought stress index (SFD). On the other hand, it seems that it is more regularly competition and/or soil conductivity that structure water stress indicators (WP, HSM). [SOURCE: Page_157]

Chapitre 3 [SOURCE: Page_167]

165 [SOURCE: Page_167]

Avant-propos [SOURCE: Page_168]

Dans l’objectif de d’affiner encore notre compréhension des mécanismes expliquant la réponse des arbres à la sécheresse dans les forêts mélangées, nous avons, dans ce troisième chapitre, exploré les déterminants du stress hydrique à l'échelle individuelle, en ré-analysant les données acquises lors du premier chapitre. Nous avons en particulier quantifié l’importance de la structure du voisinage, ainsi que de l’identité fonctionnelle de l’arbre cible et du voisinage. Pour ceci nous avons collecté des données d’inventaire pour chacun des sites et calculé différents indices de compétitions pour tester l’effet de la structure sur le potentiel hydrique. Nous avons, par ailleurs, caractériser l’identité des arbres voisins et de l’arbre cible, en utilisant des traits fonctionnels. Les résultats montrent que l'identité fonctionnelle des espèces est le facteur principal expliquant le stress hydrique des arbres en période de sécheresse extrême. Une approche multi-trait basée sur une analyse en composante principale améliore significativement la prédiction du stress hydrique par rapport aux approches mono-trait. Par ailleurs, la diversité spécifique n'a pas d'effet direct sur le stress hydrique, mais elle module l'influence de la structure du voisinage. Par exemple, il semblerait qu’un voisinage plus diversifié composé d'espèces peu vulnérables à la cavitation réduise le stress hydrique des arbres de grande taille. Ces résultats suggèrent que combiner différents traits fonctionnels permet de décrire et rationaliser l’effet prédominant de l’identité taxonomique sur la réponse physiologique des arbres à une sécheresse extrême. Nos résultats suggèrent aussi que prendre en compte l’identité fonctionnelle des arbres composant le voisinage, conjointement avec sa structure, permet d’affiner notre compréhension des effets du mélange d’espèces sur la réponse des arbres à la sécheresse. La discussion générale de ce manuscrit reprend l’ensemble des résultats de cette thèse et les compare à la littérature actuelle du domaine. Nous pointons les apports que cette thèse a permis mais aussi les limites de ce travail. Enfin nous proposons des perspectives d’amélioration ou d’extension de ce travail et des axes de recherche qui apparaissent pertinents à explorer dans le futur. [SOURCE: Page_168]

166 [SOURCE: Page_168]

1.     A l’échelle individuelle : L’identité fonctionnelle de l’espèce, la taille de l’arbre et la structure du voisinage interagissent pour déterminer le stress hydrique des arbres. [SOURCE: Page_169]

Introduction Les écosystèmes forestiers du monde entier subissent des sécheresses plus fréquentes et plus intenses en raison du changement climatique (Trenberth et al., 2014), ce qui est associé à une mortalité accrue des arbres (Allen et al., 2010; Hammond et al., 2022) et affecte de plus en plus les fonctions et les services forestiers (Anderegg et al., 2013; Hammond et al., 2022). L'augmentation de la diversité des espèces d'arbres est considérée comme une option de gestion importante pour adapter les forêts au changement climatique (Messier et al., 2022). Les effets de la diversité des espèces d'arbres sur les réponses des arbres à la sécheresse ont été de plus en plus étudiés dans des méta-analyses ou dans des études de terrain à grande échelle, mais les résultats sont encore controversés (Decarsin et al., 2024; Grossiord, 2020). Une étude de synthèse basée sur des données de flux de sève a montré que l'effet des mélanges d'espèces sur le stress de la sécheresse dépend de l'intensité de la sécheresse (Haberstroh and Werner, 2022), car les effets positifs de la diversité trouvés dans des conditions humides et une sécheresse relativement modérée pourraient devenir délétères lors d'événements extrêmes en raison de l'augmentation de la concurrence (Shovon et al., 2024). En utilisant les marges de sécurité hydrauliques mesurées pendant une sécheresse extrême (un indice du risque de mortalité) sur différents sites européens, Decarsin et al., 2024 ont montré que l'identité des espèces détermine le stress dû à la sécheresse ; mais aussi que la composition des espèces - plus que la richesse en espèces - peut fortement influencer l'ampleur du stress dû à la sécheresse des arbres en ayant soit un fort effet positif, soit un fort effet négatif dans certains cas. Cependant, nous ne comprenons toujours pas les déterminants du stress hydrique d’un arbre (Trugman et al., 2021), et ainsi, comment et quel type de mélange pourrait atténuer le stress dû à la sécheresse. Ceci est probablement dû au fait que de multiples facteurs interagissent pour façonner le stress [SOURCE: Page_169]

167 [SOURCE: Page_169]

hydrique à l'échelle d'un arbre individuel. Plusieurs facteurs sont en jeu. Tout d'abord, il a été démontré que l'identité de l'espèce est efficace pour expliquer le stress dû à la sécheresse dans une gamme de forêts plantées comprenant des monocultures et des mélanges (Decarsin et al., 2024). Plus précisément, des travaux récents en écophysiologie postulent que l'identité fonctionnelle d'un arbre - qui peut être définie comme un ensemble de traits hydrauliques spécifiques à l'espèce - déterminera la dynamique de dessiccation pendant une sécheresse (Choat et al., 2018). Deuxièmement, la combinaison d'espèces ayant des fonctions d'utilisation de l'eau différentes semble jouer un rôle important. En effet, des expériences contrôlées menées récemment sur de jeunes arbres en pot ont montré que la combinaison de deux espèces aux caractéristiques hydrauliques contrastées (c'est-à-dire le niveau d'isohydricité) pouvait atténuer le stress dû à la sécheresse, au moins pour l'une des deux espèces, tandis que l'effet pour l'autre espèce peut être neutre (Moreno et al., 2024) ou négatif (Bello et al., 2019; Eugénie Mas et al., 2024). Cela suggère que le stress de sécheresse d'un arbre est également influencé par l'identité fonctionnelle (en termes d'utilisation de l'eau et de résistance à la sécheresse : c'est-à-dire les traits hydrauliques) de son voisin. D'autres travaux ont également souligné que la taille de l'arbre et plus généralement la structure du voisinage d'un arbre peuvent avoir un effet important sur le stress lié à la sécheresse (Trugman et al., 2021). Ceci peut être hérité de ses stratégies écologiques (utilisation des ressources) mais aussi de la stratégie écologique du voisin, peut prédire les effets du mélange d'espèces sur les schémas d'utilisation de l'eau de l'arbre (article sap flow, Decarsin et al., in prep ; (Guillemot and Martin-StPaul, 2024; E. Mas et al., 2024; Eugénie Mas et al., 2024). Les indices de taille des arbres ainsi que les indices caractérisant la structure voisine ont le potentiel d'être de bons indicateurs du stress dû à la sécheresse. Il est donc possible d'émettre l'hypothèse que, à l'échelle d'un arbre individuel, différents facteurs déterminent le stress dû à la sécheresse lors d'une sécheresse extrême, notamment : (1) L'identité fonctionnelle de l'arbre qui peut être résumée à l'aide de différents traits souvent mesurés au niveau de l'espèce. (2) la taille de l'arbre, (3) le voisinage de l'arbre qui peut être approximé par différents indices tels que l'indice de compétition. En outre, ces indices peuvent être modifiés pour tenir compte des propriétés fonctionnelles de l'espèce. Dans cette étude, nous avons cherché à explorer les facteurs qui déterminent le stress de la sécheresse au niveau de l'arbre sur 14 espèces plantées sur quatre sites expérimentaux répartis en Europe où la diversité a été manipulée au 168 [SOURCE: Page_170]

niveau de la plantation. Nous avons pris en compte l'identité fonctionnelle des espèces en compilant une base de données de traits hydrauliques et nous avons utilisé l'inventaire forestier pour calculer divers indices de compétition afin de caractériser le voisinage. Nous émettons l'hypothèse que (1) l'identité fonctionnelle de l'arbre, la taille de l'arbre et la structure du voisinage de l'arbre joueront un rôle majeur, en interaction, dans la formation du stress de sécheresse au niveau de l'arbre. [SOURCE: Page_171]

Matériel et Méthode [SOURCE: Page_171]

Designs expérimentaux [SOURCE: Page_171]

Cette étude a été menée dans cinq sites expérimentaux dédiés à l’étude des effets de la diversité des arbres sur le fonctionnement des forêts situées dans des biomes contrastées (aux conditions climatiques et pédologiques différentes) en Europe occidentale et méridionale (voir Figure 1 du chapitre 1) dans le cadre du réseau TreeDivNet (Verheyen et al., 2016), voir Decarsin et al., 2024 pour plus de détails sur les conditions climatiques et les spécificités des sites expérimentaux. Toutes les expériences comprennent des espèces d'arbres cultivées à la fois en monoculture et en mélange dans un plan randomisé répété qui permet de tester l'effet de la diversité des arbres sur le fonctionnement des écosystèmes forestiers. Les expériences étudiées comprennent ORPHEE en France, IDENT-Freiburg en Allemagne, FORBIO- Gedinne en Belgique, IDENT-Macomer en Italie et BTREE en Autriche (tableau 1). Les espèces d'arbres cultivées dans le cadre de ces expériences ont été sélectionnées car elles sont localement largement utilisées dans le milieu forestier ou dans l’aménagement urbain. Table 1. strobus, Pinus sylvestris, Quercus robur, Quercus rubra [SOURCE: Page_173]

La densité de plantation allait de 2500 arbres par hectare sur le site expérimental d’ORPHEE à 62500 arbres par hectare à IDENT-Macomer. Dans chaque expérience, nous avons sélectionné des parcelles le long d'un gradient de richesse en espèces (mélanges de 1 à 6 espèces). Toutes les espèces étudiées ont été échantillonnées à la fois dans des mélanges et des monocultures. Au total, 21 espèces différentes, 43 compositions d'espèces différentes (21 monocultures et 22 mélanges) ont été étudiées. Toutes ont été mesurées pour le stress hydrique. L'âge des arbres au moment de l'échantillonnage variait d'une expérience à l'autre, allant de 8 (IDENT- Macomer) à 14 ans (ORPHEE). Les arbres échantillonnés étaient dominants ou codominants et n'avaient que des voisins vivants. La hauteur moyenne des arbres variait considérablement entre les espèces et les expériences, allant de 0,7 m (Phillyrea latifolia à IDENT-Macomer) à 11,8 m (Pinus pinaster à ORPHEE et Larix x eurolepsis à FORBIO-Gedinne). Les arbres ont été échantillonnés dans la partie intérieure des parcelles, et nous avons évité d'échantillonner des arbres proches les uns des autres. [SOURCE: Page_173]

Potentiel hydrique de base [SOURCE: Page_173]

Nous avons cherché à mesurer le stress hydrique dans des conditions de sécheresse extrême dans les différents sites expérimentaux. Pour ce faire, nous avons effectué des mesures au cours d'années exceptionnellement sèches dans les différentes expériences, comme dans Decarsin et al. 2024 (Chapitre 1, été 2022). En outre, nous avons cherché à échantillonner chaque expérience au moment du pic saisonnier d'intensité de la sécheresse. La date d'échantillonnage a été planifiée un ou deux jours avant les mesures, sur la base des prévisions météorologiques, afin d'effectuer l'échantillonnage à la fin d'une longue période de sécheresse et juste avant le début des précipitations automnales. L'intensité extrême de la sécheresse de l'année et du jour des mesures a été confirmée par la suite à l'aide de simulations du potentiel hydrique du sol à partir du modèle hydraulique des plantes basé sur les [SOURCE: Page_173]

171 [SOURCE: Page_173]

caractéristiques, SurEau (Ruffault et al., 2022; voir la figure 1 et le matériel supplémentaire S$_2$ du chapitre 1). Dans chaque expérience, les mesures ont été effectuées au cours de deux ou trois journées ensoleillées consécutives afin de garantir des conditions météorologiques comparables. Les feuilles ou les pousses de la canopée des arbres ont été prélevées à l'aide d'élagueurs. Ψpd a été mesuré dans un créneau de deux heures avant le lever du soleil. Quatre arbres ont été échantillonnés par espèce et par parcelle, et deux blocs ont été échantillonnés (soit un total de n=8 mesures pour chaque espèce dans chaque niveau de diversité) dans tous les sites expérimentaux. Les échantillons ont été immédiatement scellés dans des sacs en plastique Ziplock après avoir soufflé dedans pour les saturer d'humidité. Les échantillons ont ensuite été placés dans une glacière portable (en évitant tout contact avec de la glace) dans l'obscurité avant d'être mesurés avec la bombe à pression de Scholander directement sur le terrain (c'est-à-dire moins d'une demi- heure après l'échantillonnage, Rodriguez-Dominguez et al., 2022). [SOURCE: Page_174]

Traits physiologiques [SOURCE: Page_174]

Nous avons mesuré la vulnérabilité à la cavitation du xylème (P50) de la même manière que dans Decarsin et al., 2024. Nous avons ensuite récupéré de la littérature le TLP, le SLA ainsi que la densité du bois des différentes espèces étudiées de la même manière que dans Serrano Leon et al., soumis dans Global Change Biology en Novembre 2024 « Supplementary Method 3. Functional traits sélection ». [SOURCE: Page_174]

Les indicateurs de la structure locale du voisinage [SOURCE: Page_174]

Pour nous permettre d’obtenir des indicateurs de la structure du voisinage (NSE = Neighbour structure effect) nous avons dérivé le package de simulation végétale spatialement explicite à l’échelle individuelle « siplab ». La fonction ‘’pairwise‘’ de ce package permet de calculer des indices de compétition classiques en intégrant des données spatiales et des données d’inventaire (diamètre, hauteur, taille de couronne, …). Cette fonction utilise des fonctions équations spécifiques aux indices souhaités que l’on appelle ‘’kernel’’. Nous avons modifié la fonction ‘’pairwise’’ pour qu’elle soit capable de calculer, en plus d’un indice indifférencié global, des indices pour chacune des espèces présentes dans le voisinage. Ainsi nous sommes capables de scinder l’influence des individus du voisinage selon qu’il s’agit d’interaction intraspécifiques et interspécifiques. Cette modification de fonctionnalité implique, lorsque l’on souhaite [SOURCE: Page_174]

172 [SOURCE: Page_174]

l’utiliser, que l’on n’utilise uniquement des indices au caractère additif. Effectivement on se repose sur l’additivité des effets de chaque individu du voisinage pour parvenir à différencier l’effet de chaque espèce du voisinage séparément. Nous avons enfin recodé des ‘’kernels’’ spécifiques aux indices que nous souhaitions calculer. Nous avons travaillé sur de multiples indices caractérisant la structure de voisinage résumé par Curto et al., 2020, table^1. Parmi leurs indices nous avons sélectionné ceux que l’on pouvait calculer avec nos données d’inventaire ainsi que les indices qui étaient additifs. Analyses statistiques [SOURCE: Page_177]

Évaluer la contribution du la structure du voisinage, de la diversité spécifique, de la taille et de l’identité fonctionnelle de l’individu cibles sur son stress hydrique Dans Decarsin et al., 2024 nous avons inclus, à l’échelle des 5 sites étudiés, une analyse visant à évaluer comment la surface terrière et la taille des individus influencent l’effet de la diversité sur la P50, le potentiel hydrique et la HSM. A ce moment nous n’avions pas réalisé d'analyse à l’échelle individuelle car il ne s’agissait pas de l’objectif premier et que la structure des données du site IDENT-Macomer ne nous permettait pas d’avoir des données à cette échelle. Dans cette analyse nous devrons donc exclure le site expérimental de IDENT-Macomer pour pousser nos analyses à l’échelle individuelle. Pour comparer les valeurs des individus des différents sites nous avons standardisé les données à l’échelle du site expérimental. <- < L’ensemble des variables ont été standardisées ( ? ). Nous avons utilisé des modèles 6 [SOURCE: Page_177]

linéaires (ANOVA, « car » R package, Fox et al., 2012) pour évaluer et comparer l’effet, à la fois de traits physiologiques (PCA$_1$, PCA$_2$, HSM_tlp, P50, TLP, SLA and Wood density) et des 8 indices de structure du voisinage présentés précédemment, sur la performance de multiples modèles (Eq 1-5). L’effet du diamètre des individus (D), de différents traits de l’espèce, de différents indices de la structure du voisinage (NSE) et l’indice de diversité de Shannon (DIV) ont été testés et sont comparés dans ces résultats. ᴪ23 ~ (𝐷 + 𝑁𝑆𝐸 + 𝐷𝐼𝑉)^2                (1) [SOURCE: Page_177]

Pour chacun des traits (PCA$_1$, PCA$_2$, HSM_tlp, P50, TLP, Wood density et SLA) nous avons sélectionné l’indice de structure du voisinage permettant une meilleure performance du modèle. L’exposant carré dans la description des modèles signifie [SOURCE: Page_177]

175 [SOURCE: Page_177]

qu’ils incluent toutes les interactions deux à deux entre variables. Pour ceci nous avons utilisé, pour chaque indice de structure du voisinage, la méthodologie de sélection de modèles avec la fonction Dredge du package R ‘’MuMIn’’. Lors de ce processus de sélection, l’ensemble des combinaisons de variables du modèle sont classés par delta-AICc. Nous sélectionnons alors le modèle le plus parcimonieux comme étant celui ayant le plus fort Akaike-weight parmi les modèles ayant un delta- AICc inférieur à 2. Finalement nous sélectionnons pour chaque trait le modèle parmi les huit présélectionnés celui ayant le plus petit AICc. Pour limiter l’autocorrélation entre les variables explicatives nous avons (en amont du “Dredge”) testé et ajusté chaque modèle en utilisant le critère VIF (Variance inflation factor) calculé avec la fonction ‘’vif’’ du package ‘’car’’. Lorsque le score vif est supérieur à 5 la variable correspondante est enlevée du modèle. Évaluer la contribution de la structure du voisinage, de la composition fonctionnelle du voisinage et de la taille de l’arbre cible sur son stress hydrique Dans l’objectif de focaliser notre analyse sur l’effet des conditions locales du voisinage nous avons utilisé des modèles linéaires mixtes, en utilisant la fonction lmer du package “lme^4”, incluant un paramètre aléatoire décrivant une structure hiérarchique. Effectivement, la différence entre les sites expérimentaux est supposée faible puisque nous avons échantillonné au pic de la sécheresse au cours de la même année. Certes, les sites expérimentaux sont éloignés géographiquement les uns des autres mais le potentiel hydrique du sol au moment des mesures est similaire comme montré dans la figure 1 de Decarsin et al., 2024. De plus, nous avons choisi de faire ceci car l’identité de l'espèce cible est un paramètre primordial à considérer dans l’étude du stress hydrique comme montré dans Decarsin et al., 2024 ainsi que via la performance bien plus élevée observée du modèle 2 (voir tableau 3). Dans cette analyse nous avons comparé deux modèles considérant trois variables à l’échelle de l’individu. Puisque le trait spécifique permettant une meilleure performance des modèles utilisant un trait fonctionnel de l’espèce cible est la P50 (voir modèle 3, tableau 3) nous avons décidé d’utiliser la structure du voisinage locale pondéré par la stratégie écologique des espèces en présentes (𝐶𝑊𝑀79$A$_7$ ) utilisant ce même trait. La 𝐶𝑊𝑀.)L représente ici la structure du voisinage local selon l’indice DII$_7$ (voir tableau 2 pour plus de détails) modulé par la capacité de résistance à la cavitation des espèces présentes dans le [SOURCE: Page_178]

176 [SOURCE: Page_178]

voisinage. Plus les espèces en interaction sont résistantes à la cavitation plus la 𝐶𝑊𝑀.)L augmente. Définition des models (function lmer in R) : •   𝑃𝑏𝑎𝑠𝑒 ~ (𝐷 + 𝐷𝐼𝑉 + 𝑁𝑆𝐸 )^2 + 𝑑A + 𝜀                      (10) •   𝑃𝑏𝑎𝑠𝑒 ~ (𝐷 + 𝐷𝐼𝑉 + 𝐶𝑊𝑀.)L )^2 + 𝑑A + 𝜀 (11) [SOURCE: Page_179]

Où D représente le diamètre, DIV la diversité avec l’indice de shannon, NSE et 𝐶𝑊𝑀.)L représente l’indice de structure locale du voisinage, 𝑑A correspond à un effet aléatoire hiérarchisé de l’espèce dans chacun des sites expérimentaux et 𝜀 les résidus. [SOURCE: Page_179]

Résultats : [SOURCE: Page_179]

La diversité spécifique module l’effet de la structure sur le stress hydrique des peuplements mélangés [SOURCE: Page_179]

Chacun des modèles incluant une variable de trait expliquait mieux les variations de potentiel hydrique que celui n’en incluant pas. Bien que les R$_2$ des différents modèles étaient faibles, ils étaient systématiquement meilleurs en considérant un trait physiologique. Lorsque l’on considérait l'identité de l’espèce (variable factorielle) à la place d’un trait physiologique nous obtenions un R$_2$ encore augmenté (+275%) par rapport au modèle incluant un trait physiologique le plus performant (modèle 6, R$_2$ = 0.206***). Ce résultat suggère que considérer la physiologie des individus est important pour comprendre et prédire le stress hydrique néanmoins un seul trait physiologique n’est qu’une part de l’identité de l’espèce. Nous avons donc remplacé la variable “trait” par la coordonnée sur les deux principaux axes d’une ACP sur les traits physiologiques des différentes espèces comme dans Guillemot et al., 2021. Le premier axe a permis d’augmenter significativement le R$_2$ du modèle comparé aux modèles n’utilisant qu’un seul trait. Le second axe en revanche n’a que très marginalement augmenté le R$_2$ comparé au modèle sans variable ajouté (modèle 1). La diversité (DIV) ne semble pas avoir d’effet direct sur le potentiel hydrique mais dans la plupart des modèles elle interagit avec les autres variables en changeant leurs effets respectifs. Le modèle 3, le modèle intégrant la composante principale de l’identité fonctionnelle des espèces étudiées, est le modèle ayant la meilleure performance (R$_2$=0.32) parmi les modèles considérant la physiologie des espèces. Dans ce [SOURCE: Page_179]

177 [SOURCE: Page_179]

modèle, la diversité spécifique, qui n’a pas d’effet direct sur le stress hydrique, réduit l’effet négatif de la structure du voisinage (NSE) sur le stress hydrique (interaction “DIV:NSE” dans le modèle 3 égale à -0.72). La structure locale du voisinage (NSE) seule était significativement explicative pour cinq modèles sur six et systématiquement explicative en interaction pour l’ensemble des modèles. On note que la plupart du temps le NSE sélectionné est la surface terrière du voisinage (NBA). Pour les deux cas considérant la coordonnée sur les axes de l’ACP un indice dépendant de la distance entre les individus fut sélectionné. Le seul modèle dans lequel on trouve un indice indépendant de la distance entre les individus (DII$_7$) est le modèle 6. Le diamètre de l’arbre s’avère être significativement explicatif pour cinq modèles sur les six testés et dans chaque cas il était en interaction avec la NSE ce qui suggère que son effet varie selon la structure locale. important. En revanche, le diamètre de l’arbre n'a pas d'effet direct significatif [SOURCE: Page_181]

(β=−0.0186±0.0155, p=0.2332). [SOURCE: Page_181]
