296      Radial growth measurements 297 [SOURCE: Page_245]

298      We obtained annual series of tree-ring width (TRW) and mean wood density using X-ray micro- 299      Computed Tomography (µCT) with the HECTOR µCT scanner (Masschaele et al. 2013) at the 300      Ghent University Centre for X-ray tomography (UGCT; http://www.ugct.ugent.be). Before 301      scanning, increment cores were dried at room temperature for one month to be in balance with 302      the scanner room environment (20 ºC, relative humidity 34 %) and mounted in master sample 303      holders for batch scanning. We scanned cores at an approximate voxel pitch resolution of 50 304      μm following the workflow for µCT densitometry detailed in de de Mil et al. (2016). 305      Reconstructions of the scanned sample batch were performed using the Octopus 306      Reconstruction software (Vlassenbroeck et al. 2007). We extracted the three-dimensional 307      images of each single core sample and converted them to density estimates using specific 308      toolboxes (van den Bulcke et al. 2014; de Mil et al. 2016; de Mil and van den Bulcke 2023). 309      Details of the methodology followed for the reconstruction, extraction and crossdating of tree 310      ring series are explained in Supplementary Method 2. Rigorous quality filtering was performed 311      to ensure that annual growth rings where correctly defined, discarding from the analysis those 312      samples with ambiguous tree ring definitions after the crossdating processing and species with 313      a substantial proportion of doubtful samples at a given site (> 40%). See Figure S$_5$ for an 314      overview of the wood anatomy of species. We analyzed a total of 948 trees from 16 species 315      and 68 different species compositions (26 monocultures, 28 simple mixtures, 14 more diverse 316      mixtures) (Table S$_2$). [SOURCE: Page_245]

317      We calculated basal area increment (BAI, mm2 year-1) series from pith to bark based on the 318      TRW series using the bai.in() function in the dplR package in R (Bunn 2008; Bunn et al. 2023). 319      We estimated an indicator for radial biomass increment (hereafter BIOMinc, kg m -1, year-1) as 320      the product of BAI and mean wood density (kg m-3) of the ring (Figure S8). This indicator at the 321      individual tree level reflects the actual carbon allocation in radial growth better than TRW and 322      BAI metrics (Camarero and Andrés 2024) and it can be considered a proxy of aboveground 323      biomass growth when continuous inventory data in annual tree height growth is missing 324      (Vannoppen et al. 2018; Bontemps et al. 2010). We systematically tested different 325      transformation and detrending options for the growth variables, but all methods resulted on 326      potential removal or overestimation of the drought-induced responses (Supplementary Method 327      2). Given the challenges to detrend age-effect in such short time series, we analyzed further 328      drought-induced growth responses based on raw and undetrended series of the tree ring 329      variables (Schwarz et al. 2020; Schnabel et al. 2024a). BIOMinc and BAI series were used as 330      a more reliable indicator of temporal trends in radial growth for young trees than TRW (i.e. less 331      influenced by biological age trends) (Biondi and Qeadan 2008). 335      where Growthyear i is the radial growth (either TRW, BAI, or BIOMinc) for the given year i 336      (drought or post-drought year) and average GrowthPreDr is the mean growth during the 337      corresponding pre-drought reference year(s) for that site (Figure S$_6$). [SOURCE: Page_246]

338 [SOURCE: Page_246]

339      Functional traits selection 340 [SOURCE: Page_246]

341      To determine the functional identity of tree species and functional diversity of neighborhoods, 342      we determined the species’ drought tolerance as the hydraulic safety margin (HSMTLP, MPa) 343      based on both stomatal traits and hydraulic traits to encompass the spectrum of processes 344      involved in drought tolerance but also resource use (Choat et al. 2012; Martin-StPaul et al. 345      2017). We defined HSMTLP as the extent to which early stomatal closure protects the xylem 346      from dysfunction during drought, calculated as the difference between the turgor loss point 347      (TLP, Mpa, a proxy of the stomatal closure point) and the water potential at which 50% of 348      xylem cavitates (P50, unit MPa) (HSMTLP = TLP − P50). This HSMTLP definition has been used 349      to predict the risk of drought-induced tree mortality (Martin-StPaul et al. 2017; Powers et al. 350      2020) and is linked to stomatal control as TLP correlates with leaf water potential at stomatal 351      closure (Bartlett et al. 2016; Brodribb and Holbrook 2003). HSMTLP , used as a trait 352      characterizing species’ drought tolerance, differentiates from the traditional HSM metric (based 353      on minimum water potential, Ψmin), which is considered a measure of drought stress (Choat et 354      al. 2012). We considered species-specific mean trait values from multiple consolidated 355      species-level datasets (see Supplementary Method 3 for the complete list of sources, and 356      Table S6 for the final dataset of species-specific trait values). Additionally, we assessed the 357      relation among these hydraulic traits and additional traits related to the whole-plant economics 358      spectrum (i.e. leaf mass per area, leaf nitrogen concentration, wood density) using pairwise 359      correlations and principal component analysis (PCA) (Supplementary Method 3, Table S6). 360      HSMTLP was associated with other drought-tolerance traits and aligned with the first PCA axis 361      explaining most of the variation across traits (Figure S12, Figure S13). Finally, we compared 362      the effect of HSMTLP and additional functional traits on the growth responses during a single- 363      year drought with a sensitivity analysis among different linear mixed-effect models as a function 364      of each species-specific trait (Supplementary Method 4, Table S7, Figure S14). 368      Neighborhood competition and tree diversity 369 370      We defined neighborhoods of focal trees as all alive direct (first-order) neighbors and second- 371      order neighbors that had crowns interacting with the focal tree’s crown within a certain 372      neighborhood radius. This neighborhood radius was adapted to each site to account for the 373      differences in planting density and design between experiments i.e. radius 2.9 m for most sites 374      with larger planting distance, radius 1.5 m for sites with narrow planting distance (B-Tree, 375      IDENT-Freiburg, IDENT-Macomer) (Figure S$_4$, Table S$_5$). We measured diameter of each 376      focal and neighbor tree with a digital caliper at 1 mm resolution at the same coring height and 377      direction. For each neighboring tree, we recorded its relative position to the focal tree and 378      species identity. We quantified competition experienced by focal trees at the time of coring 379      using these measured neighborhood data, except for IDENT-Freiburg and IDENT-Macomer 380      for which we used inventory data from the same year. The spatial definition of the tree 381      neighborhood around each focal tree was done using the sf R-package (Pebesma and Bivand 382      2023). The distance-dependent Hegyi’s index (Hegyi 1974)was calculated as a competition 383      index for each focal tree using the following equation: [SOURCE: Page_247]

𝐵𝐴𝑗 ⁄𝐵𝐴𝑖 384                𝐻𝑒𝑔𝑦𝑖𝑖 = ∑𝑛𝑗=1          𝑑𝑖𝑗 [SOURCE: Page_247]

385      where BAi and BAj are the basal area of the focal tree i and each tree neighbor j respectively, 386      and dij is the distance between each tree neighbor and the focal tree, considering all n direct 387      neighbor trees (from all species) within a given focal tree’s neighborhood. Alternative 388      competition indices based on height were not considered as height data was not available for 389      all neighborhood trees. [SOURCE: Page_247]

390      Neighborhood tree diversity was considered as the realized neighborhood species richness 391      (nSR) and the functional diversity of HSMTLP (FDHSM). FDHSM for each focal tree’s neighborhood 392      (community) was calculated as the abundance-weighted functional dispersion as described by 393      Laliberté and Legendre (2010) using the FD R-package (Laliberté et al. 2014): [SOURCE: Page_247]

∑𝑛 𝑘=1 𝐵𝐴𝑘 𝑑𝑘 394                𝐹𝐷𝐻𝑆𝑀 =        ∑𝑛 𝑘=1 𝑑𝑘 [SOURCE: Page_247]

395      where BAk is the relative abundance of species k in a neighborhood with n species, calculated 396      as the cumulative basal area, and dk is the distance in the traits space of species k to the 397      weighted centroid of the neighborhood community. Functional dispersion measures the mean [SOURCE: Page_247]

402      Statistical analysis 403 [SOURCE: Page_248]

404      To answer research questions Q$_1$ and Q$_3$ in relation to the single-year drought response 405      across all sites, we used linear mixed-effect models (LMMs) of the drought-induced growth 406      responses during the first drought year to test the direct effect of neighborhood tree diversity 407      (Q$_1$) and its interaction with drought-tolerance (HSMTLP) of the focal-tree species (tree diversity 408      x HSMTLP, Q$_3$). We tested the effects of neighborhood tree diversity in separate models for the 409      moderators nSR (m^1a) and FDHSM (m^1b) using the same basic model structure. To account 410      for the experimental design and differences between sites, we used a nested group-level 411      (random) effect structure of plot nested within site. We also tested for extended versions of the 412      model, by considering the three-way interaction effects of tree diversity, drought tolerance and 413      the following predictors: neighborhood competition (tree diversity x HSMTLP x Hegyi), tree basal 414      area (tree diversity x HSMTLP x BA), drought intensity in terms of SPEI12 (tree diversity x 415      HSMTLP x SPEI12), drought intensity in terms of SPEI6sept (tree diversity x HSMTLP x 416      SPEI6sept), and drought intensity in terms of minimum monthly REW during the growing 417      season (tree diversity x HSMTLP x REW). [SOURCE: Page_248]

418      To answer Q2 and Q3 regarding consecutive drought years, we used site-specific models to 419      analyze growth responses considering the subset of six experiments that experienced a multi- 420      year drought event. These models evaluated drought-induced growth responses across 421      consecutive years as a function of all two-way interactions between the response year, HSMTLP 422      of the focal-tree species and the neighborhood tree diversity. Analyzing Q2 was based on the 423      interaction tree diversity x Resp_yr, whereas analyzing Q3 was based on the interactions 424      HSMTLP x tree diversity and HSMTLP x Resp_yr. We tested the effects of neighborhood tree 425      diversity in separate models for the moderators nSR (m2a) and FDHSM (m2b) using the same 426      basic model structure. We accounted for non-linear drought responses across consecutive 427      years including Resp_yr as a categorical fixed effect (Resp_yr 1, 2 and 3 for the consecutive 428      drought years, Resp_yr 4 for the post-drought year). Models to address Q2 were fitted 429      considering an intercept 0 as reference for pre-drought and included individual tree as a 430      random effect intercept. Here, we did not consider drought intensity (i.e. SPEI) as fixed effect 431      since it would confound the fixed effect of the consecutive Resp_yr. We used tree individual 432      as random effect to account for the multiple Resp_yr observations per tree. [SOURCE: Page_248]

433      All models addressing Q$_1$ and Q$_2$ used a log transformation of the response variables to meet 434      model assumptions (normality and heteroscedasticity). All models controlled for fixed effects 435      of tree basal area (scaled to account for relative intraspecific differences in tree size within 436      each site and species) and competition (standardized to account for relative interspecific 437      competition within each site). Standardization of model predictors (to meet model assumptions 438      and have comparable effect sizes across sites) and testing of alternative random structures 439      are detailed in Supplementary Method 5. We compared the model performance and parsimony 440      of fixed effects among the separate models based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). 441      The presentation of model results focusses on growth responses in terms of BIOMinc (Table 442      S$_8$). All analyses were computed using R version 4.3.1 (R Core Team 2023). All models were 443      fitted using lme^4 package (Bates et al. 2015) with restricted maximum likelihood estimation 444      (REML). Model statistics and marginal effects were visualized using sjPlot package (Lüdecke 445      et al. 2024). [SOURCE: Page_249]

446 [SOURCE: Page_249]

447      Results 448 [SOURCE: Page_249]

449      Growth responses during a single-year drought 450 [SOURCE: Page_249]

451      We observed substantial variability in growth responses within each site, indicating that not all 452      trees reduced growth during a single extreme drought year compared to pre-drought conditions 453      (Figure 3, Figure S$_9$). Models showed that drought-induced growth responses during the a 454      single-year drought were significantly influenced by the focal-species HSMTLP (p < 0.001) 455      (Figure 3, Table S$_9$). Overall, species with high HSMTLP had less growth reduction compared 456      to species with lower HSMTLP. The positive HSMTLP effect was modulated by drought intensity 457      (HSMTLP x REW, p < 0.01), although this modulation was only significant when using REW, 458      not SPEI indices (Table S$_9$). Reduction in growth in low HSMTLP species was more pronounced 459      at sites experiencing the most extreme drought intensity (REW = 0), where differences 460      between species with contrasting HSMTLP were higher. Drought-tolerant species showed 461      similar growth responses at sites with less extreme drought conditions (REW = 0.03), where 462      differences with low-HSMTLP species were less pronounced. [SOURCE: Page_249]

463      The model considering the 3-way interaction between FDHSM x HSMTLP x REW was the most 464      parsimonious (lowest AIC) and with highest explanatory power (conditional R2 = 0.50, marginal 465      R2 of fixed effects = 0.26). Nevertheless, there was no evidence that growth responses during 466      a single-year drought were influenced by neighborhood tree diversity, either in terms of nSR [SOURCE: Page_249]

467      or FDHSM (Figure 4, Table S$_9$). Additionally, no interaction was found between tree diversity 468      and HSMTLP, as species with contrasting HSMTLP responded similarly to increasing tree 469      diversity. Likewise, there was no significant interaction effect between tree diversity and 470      drought intensity, whether in terms of REW or SPEI indices. Single-year drought responses 471      were also not influenced by relative neighborhood competition, either directly or in interaction 472      with HSMTLP and tree diversity (tree diversity x HSMTLP x Hegyi) (Figure 4, Table S$_9$, Table 473      S10). In contrast, all models showed a positive direct effect of tree size (relative intraspecific 474      differences) on the drought response (p < 0.01), although tree size did not modulate the 475      interaction with HSMTLP or tree diversity. Within each species, trees with larger BA consistently 476      had more positive drought responses. [SOURCE: Page_250]

508      Growth responses during consecutive drought years 509 [SOURCE: Page_252]

510      In site-specific models of multi-year drought events, we observed that the effects of 511      neighborhood tree diversity on growth responses strengthened over consecutive drought years 512      at most sites (interaction tree diversity x Resp_yr) (Figure 5, Table S11, Table S12). While no 513      site showed significant diversity effects during the initial severe drought year (Resp_yr 1), 514      diversity effects emerged during subsequent drought years and the post-drought year (Figure 515      S$_3$, Table S$_4$). The direction and magnitude of diversity effects on growth responses over 516      consecutive drought years varied by site. A positive diversity effect was evident only at IDENT- 517      Freiburg (p < 0.001), where higher diversity increased relative growth during the following 518      consecutive drought years (Resp_yr 2-3) and post-drought (Resp_yr 4). In contrast, a negative 519      effect of functional diversity was evident during the third drought year (Resp_yr 3) at FORBIO- 520      Zedelgem (p < 0.001) and Satakunta (p < 0.01), intensifying even under favorable conditions 521      in the post-drought year at these sites (p < 0.001) and at BIOTREE-Kaltenborn (p < 0.01). A 522      neutral effect of neighborhood tree diversity across consecutive years was found at FORBIO- 523      Gedinne and FORBIO-Hechtel-Eksel. At all sites, tree diversity increased growth response 524      variability. Models based on FDHSM were more parsimonious (lower AIC) and with higher 525      proportion of variance explained (marginal R$_2$ ranging between 0.05 for Satakunta and 0.38 526      for IDENT-Freiburg) than models based on species richness (Table S11, Table S12). [SOURCE: Page_252]

527      Regarding the drought tolerance traits, no models showed significant interaction between tree 528      diversity (nSR, FDHSM) and HSMTLP, indicating that species with contrasting HSMTLP were not 529      affected differently by increased diversity. However, the effect of HSMTLP on growth responses 530      varied depending on the site (Figure 6, Table S11, Table S12). A positive HSMTLP effect across 531      response years was only moderately evident at FORBIO-Zedelgem (p < 0.05), while most sites 532      show no significant effect during the first drought year (unlike in the Q$_1$ model). Nevertheless, 533      drought-tolerant species with higher HSMTLP generally showed improved growth in the post- 534      drought year (Resp_yr 4) at FORBIO-Gedinne, FORBIO-Hechtel-Eksel (p < 0.001), IDENT- 535      Freiburg and Satakunta (p < 0.01). Conversely, at BIOTREE-Kaltenborn, drought-tolerant 536      species had lower relative growth during the consecutive drought and post-drought years 537      (Resp_yr 2-4) compared to species with lower HSMTLP (p < 0.001). [SOURCE: Page_252]

575      Discussion 576 [SOURCE: Page_255]

577      Tree diversity effects on growth responses are strengthened over 578      consecutive drought years 579 580      We found that increasing neighborhood tree diversity, whether quantified through species 581      richness or hydraulic trait diversity, had a neutral effect on the growth responses during a 582      single-year drought (Q1, Figure 4). This aligns with studies reporting mixed or neutral tree 583      diversity effects during mild droughts, which can turn to negative effects during severe droughts 584      (Haberstroh and Werner 2022; Grossiord et al. 2014b; Anderegg et al. 2013). However, we did 585      not observe any significant interaction between tree diversity and drought intensity in radial 586      growth responses during the first drought year. It is possible that those effects may not be 587      evident as changes in radial growth during a single-year drought, even if physiological 588      processes (i.e. stomatal regulation of water use) are strongly affected by drought (Jucker et al. 589      2017; Schnabel et al. 2022). The reason for this is that radial growth can remain stable if trees 590      mobilize carbon reserves from previous years to sustain growth under initial drought conditions 591      (Cailleret et al. 2017; Körner 2019; McDowell et al. 2022). However, our study data cannot 592      ascertain whether these mechanisms played a role. 593 594      Although diversity effects were absent in the first drought year, tree diversity effects on site- 595      specific growth responses strengthened during consecutive drought years and persisted into 596      the post-drought year (Q2, Figure 5). Interestingly, the direction of this effect varied across 597      sites: three sites showed increasingly negative diversity effects, two showed neutral effects, 598      and one showed a positive effect. This corroborates the contrasting and site-specific diversity 599      effects reported in earlier studies (Ratcliffe et al. 2017; Forrester et al. 2016; Grossiord 2020). 600      Notably, our study is unique in showing these different response patterns across multiple [SOURCE: Page_255]

601      experimental sites with manipulated gradients of tree species richness. The observed 602      strengthening of tree diversity effects during consecutive years could indicate an intensification 603      of tree-tree interactions under prolonged drought stress (Forrester et al. 2016; Soliveres et al. 604      2015; Maestre et al. 2009) or carry over diversity effects through drought legacy mechanisms 605      (Anderegg et al. 2015; Vilonen et al. 2022; Bastos et al. 2020). 606 607      While the observed site-specific diversity effects during multiyear drought supported both 608      proposed theoretical pathways (Figure 1), the underlying mechanisms driving these effects 609      may be highly context-dependent. Positive effects in the IDENT-Freiburg experiment align with 610      the pathway where functional diversity increasingly buffers drought stress during consecutive 611      drought years. However, only species with comparably high- HSMTLP were analyzed within this 612      experiment. In a previous study at this experiment assessing only the initial drought year 613      considered in our study, Hajek et al. (2022) found that species with higher HSM suffered less 614      and tended to decrease the survival probability of their neighbors with low HSM, and vice 615      versa. This suggests that thepositive effects observed here may result from selection effects 616      leading to a competitive release of drought-tolerant species which profit from mortality suffered 617      by drought-sensitive species (Grossiord 2020; Forrester and Bauhus 2016). Segregation of 618      tree communities into 'winner' and 'loser' species in terms of diversity was also found in another 619      tree diversity experiment under the same 2018-2020 drought (Sachsenmaier et al. 2024). As 620      drought-sensitive species decline under intensifying water competition, positive diversity 621      effects may increase for drought-tolerant species under prolonged drought stress (Maestre et 622      al. 2009). 623 624      Conversely, negative diversity effects on growth observed in three sites support the pathway 625      that prolonged drought stress can intensify with increasing functional diversity. Increased 626      stress may result from greater water consumption in mixed-species stands compared to 627      monocultures due to complementary resource-use strategies (Haberstroh and Werner 2022), 628      early overyielding of tree biomass under favorable conditions (Jump et al. 2017; Jacobs et al. 629      2021), or selection of species with high water demands (Grossiord 2020; Forrester and Bauhus 630      2016). In the FORBIO-Zedelgem experiment, complementarity and selection effects were 631      reported to drive early growth overyielding, enhancing canopy packing and stand transpiration 632      (van de Peer et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2024). This positive diversity effects under favorable 633      conditions could have negative impacts under increasing drought stress, when microclimate 634      offsets from tree mixing might be insufficient to counteract drought stress (Zhang et al. 2022). 635      In the Satakunta experiment, tree diversity did not enhance aboveground productivity or 636      transpiration under non-limiting water availability (Grossiord et al. 2013). However, boreal 637      forests with similar tree diversity showed higher water use efficiency and stomatal regulation [SOURCE: Page_256]

638      than monocultures under drier conditions, indicating that species interactions can reduce soil 639      moisture (Grossiord et al. 2014a). While complementarity in stomatal regulation, below-ground 640      complementarity and water redistribution can mitigate drought impact to some extent (Bello et 641      al. 2019; Moreno et al. 2024), these mechanisms may be overridden under severe or 642      prolonged droughts (Grossiord et al. 2019; Mas et al. 2024b). 643 644 [SOURCE: Page_257]

645      Hydraulic trait identity determines growth responses to drought 646 647      HSMTLP of focal species did not influence how tree diversity affected the growth responses 648      during either a single-year drought or consecutive droughts (Q3). Species with contrasting 649      HSMTLP showed similar responses to increased tree diversity (Figure 3), differing from studies 650      suggesting that drought-vulnerable species benefit more from higher species richness 651      (Fichtner et al. 2020; Schnabel et al. 2024a; Sachsenmaier et al. 2024). However, species with 652      high HSMTLP maintained stable growth during a single-year drought, while lower-HSMTLP 653      species showed significant reductions independently of tree diversity. These differences were 654      amplified under extreme drought, which suggests that xylem integrity under severe drought 655      allow enhanced functioning and biomass growth (Choat et al. 2012; Martin-StPaul et al. 2017; 656      Sanchez-Martinez et al. 2023; Anderegg et al. 2016). Notably, the significant interaction 657      between drought intensity and HSMTLP was evident only when using REW as a measure of 658      water availability, emphasizing the importance of quantifying local soil water conditions for 659      assessing tree drought stress over standardized climatic indices like SPEI (Zang et al. 2020; 660      Schwarz et al. 2020). 661 662      Across consecutive drought years (Figure 6), most sites showed improved relative growth in 663      the post-drought year for species with high HSMTLP, suggesting lower legacy effects for these 664      drought-tolerant species (Anderegg et al. 2015). In contrast, at BIOTREE-Kaltenborn, drought- 665      intolerant species had lower legacy effects compared to the species with higher HSMTLP, which 666      showed higher growth reductions during consecutive drought and post-drought years. 667      However, these contrasting HSMTLP effects should be interpreted cautiously, given the different 668      HSMTLP ranges between sites and limited number of species analyzed per site. Additionally, 669      species-specific mean trait values were collected from published databases, lacking site- 670      specific data on trait variability. Intraspecific trait variability at the individual tree level can 671      exceed interspecific differences (Anderegg 2015; Pritzkow et al. 2020). Trait plasticity can be 672      driven by interspecific interactions even in early tree development stages, in turn influencing 673      stand productivity and drought responses (Serrano-León et al. 2022; Benavides et al. 2019; 674      Gazol et al. 2023). To date, the only study on tree diversity effects on intra-species HSMTLP [SOURCE: Page_257]

675      variability found that HSMTLP in a subset of the experiments studied here is primarily driven by 676      species identity and not by tree diversity, though some significant diversity effects were found 677      for a limited number of species composition (Decarsin et al. 2024). The discrepancy in HSMTLP 678      effect across our sites aligns with findings that hydraulic traits do not always explain the 679      magnitude of growth declines under intense, prolonged droughts (Song et al. 2022b; Smith‐ 680      Martin et al. 2023). [SOURCE: Page_258]

681 [SOURCE: Page_258]

682      Applicability of results 683 684      A common limitation in dendrochronological studies like ours is the sampling bias toward 685      canopy-dominant trees, aimed at reducing canopy shading effects on growth responses 686      (Kannenberg et al. 2020; Duchesne et al. 2019). Although recent research shows that growth 687      responses to short-term climate variability and drought legacy effects may not differ largely 688      depending on sampling approach (Nehrbass-Ahles et al. 2014; Kannenberg et al. 2019b), 689      drought responses can differ between dominant and suppressed trees. Larger trees can be 690      less sensitive to competition for water and exhibit adaptations like greater water uptake, 691      storage capacity, and more efficient water use and transport (Fernández-de-Uña et al. 2023; 692      Colangelo et al. 2017). Our findings show that relative tree size within species has a positive 693      effect on growth responses, while neighborhood competition had no significant impact. This 694      aligns with reports that drought responses are more influenced by tree size, species identity 695      and drought characteristics than by competition (Gillerot et al. 2021; Castagneri et al. 2022; 696      Del Campo et al. 2022). We did not observe that tree size nor neighborhood competition 697      affected the interaction between tree diversity and hydraulic traits, but it should be noted that 698      our sampling strategy focused on dominant and co-dominant trees may not have captured a 699      sufficiently wide range in tree sizes to elucidate such an effect. No comprehensive study has 700      yet analyzed these factors across a tree diversity gradient including small and mid-sized trees 701      of all species across varying levels of competition. Hence, the influence of these factors on 702      tree diversity effects under drought remains unclear. [SOURCE: Page_258]

703      By using planted experiments with manipulated tree species richness, we minimized 704      confounding effects of environmental heterogeneity within each site, which often obscure 705      diversity effects in observational studies (Scherer-Lorenzen et al. 2007; Bauhus et al. 2017; 706      Pardos et al. 2021). However, observed effects in young tree diversity experiments may differ 707      from those in mature semi-natural forests, where drought responses can be influenced by tree 708      age distributions and the development of interspecific interactions with progressing succession 709      (Kambach et al. 2019; Leuschner et al. 2009). Hence, our findings are particularly relevant for [SOURCE: Page_258]

710      plantation forestry and young, intensively managed forests (Messier et al. 2022; Depauw et al. 711      2024; Camarero et al. 2021). As species interactions are expected to strengthen over time 712      (Guerrero-Ramírez et al. 2017; Jucker et al. 2017), continued monitoring of these plantations 713      will help bridge the gap between observational studies and experimental findings. [SOURCE: Page_259]

714      Our findings underscore the importance of examining tree responses over extended periods 715      to understand the effects of diversity on tree responses to drought. However, since we only 716      assessed one post-drought year, we cannot draw robust conclusions about the recovery and 717      resilience after these drought years, as drought legacy effects can persist for several years. 718      Nonetheless, our results suggest that conclusions based on single-year drought responses 719      may not hold under accelerated global warming, where prolonged drought events are 720      increasingly followed by only brief recovery periods. As climate change leads to more frequent 721      droughts, acclimation to chronic drought stress may become more crucial than recovery from 722      isolated events (Boeck et al. 2017). However, the underlying processes remain unclear. Slow 723      recovery might reflect controlled acclimation to optimize long-term survival (Gessler et al. 724      2020) or a gradual growth decline inducing tree mortality (DeSoto et al. 2020; Cailleret et al. 725      2017). Understanding the long-term impacts of consecutive droughts on forest ecosystems 726      and the role of tree diversity to mitigate chronic stress is crucial as these events become more 727      frequent. [SOURCE: Page_259]

728 [SOURCE: Page_259]

729      Conclusion 730 [SOURCE: Page_259]

731      Our study is the first to examine the role of tree diversity and functional trait identity on tree 732      growth responses across multiple experimental sites during unprecedented, multi-year 733      droughts. We demonstrated that tree diversity effects on growth responses can intensify over 734      consecutive drought years, with contrasting diversity effects varying from neutral to positive or 735      even negative effects depending on the site. The context dependency of these diversity effects 736      underlines the importance of considering multiple sites and neighborhood-scale processes in 737      understanding how interspecific interactions shape tree growth responses under prolonged 738      drought. Hydraulic traits played a significant role in determining drought-induced growth 739      responses, emphasizing the need for trait-based approaches to assess drought impacts on 740      forest ecosystems. Ultimately, integrating process-based models and hydraulic traits could 741      provide forest managers with evidence-based guidelines to design more resilient, mixed- 742      species plantations. By selecting species mixtures that are better adapted to local conditions 743      and incorporating knowledge of hydraulic traits, drought-resilient mixed plantations can be 744      used to enhance ecosystem resilience in the face of unprecedented droughts. [SOURCE: Page_259]
